Milestone 2: Data Handling & Sketches

Congestion Pricing in New York City: What Changed After the Toll?
Team 3: cyro — Praneeth Yashovardhan Kadem (pk3206), Bhavana Peruri (bp2847), Likhith Vardhan Goruputi (lvg8030)
Code: github.com/likhith2366/cyro

Overview of data handling

All data is public and is downloaded by scripts/fetch_data.py. Large tables (CRZ entries: 10-minute bins; subway: 168M hourly rows; OD estimates: 120M rows/year) are aggregated on the server with SoQL ($select ... sum() ... $group, within_polygon()) so only small summaries are downloaded. scripts/process_data.py then builds one processed table per question in data/processed/. Common steps: timestamps are treated as New York local time; hours are labelled peak (weekdays 5 a.m.-9 p.m., weekends 9 a.m.-9 p.m.) or off-peak and weekday/weekend; points (crashes, stations, Citi Bike docks) are assigned to CRZ (the MTA geofence polygon), Adjacent (within 1.5 km of the zone boundary) or Rest of NYC; seasonal effects are handled by comparing the same calendar months across years; partial months are dropped.

Datasets added since the proposal: MTA Vehicle Miles Traveled in the CBD (pre-toll baseline for Q2), MTA Subway Origin-Destination Ridership Estimates 2024/2025 (Q6), MTA CBD Geofence (zone outline) and NYC 2020 Neighbourhood Tabulation Areas (maps). Deferred: TLC trip records (the CRZ entries feed already has a TLC Taxi/FHV class). Known gaps: speeds end Aug 2025; VMT ends Jun 2026; crash data lags ~1 week; Citi Bike is one month per year so far.

Sketches: all sketches are Vega-Lite specifications rendered from the processed data (the course allows sketches made with data-viz tools). They are drafts of layout and encoding; colours, annotation and final interaction will be refined in D3/Vega-Lite for the final project.

Q1. When and where do vehicles enter the zone on a typical weekday, and which entry points are busiest?

Data: MTA CRZ Vehicle Entries (10-minute bins, Jan 5 2025 - Oct 24 2026). Transformation: summed entries server-side (SoQL) to date x hour x entry point; kept Mon-Fri; divided by the number of weekdays to get the average weekday entries per hour; summed hours for a daily total, share of all entries, and busiest hour. Each MTA detection group was given an approximate Manhattan-side coordinate for the map.

Q2. How has the number of entries changed since the toll started, by vehicle class and peak vs. off-peak?

Change from proposal: The entries dataset begins on the day the toll started, so it has no pre-toll baseline. We split the question: (a) trends since the toll, comparing the same months of 2026 vs 2025 by vehicle class and time period; (b) before vs after, using a dataset we added: MTA Vehicle Miles Traveled in the CBD (Beginning 2024).

Transformation: summed entries to date x vehicle class x time period (MTA's Peak / Overnight label); grouped to month and divided by days in the month (average daily entries); dropped incomplete months (January 2025 starts on the 5th, October 2026 is partial); compared the months present in both years (Feb-Sep). VMT is used as published (monthly average daily VMT for the zone and for the excluded roadways).

Q3. Are drivers avoiding the toll by using the FDR Drive and West Side Highway?

Transformation: four crossings report both tolled entries and excluded-roadway entries (vehicles that stay on the untolled FDR / West Side Highway): FDR at 60th, West Side Highway at 60th, Brooklyn Bridge and the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel. For each we computed excluded share = excluded / (tolled + excluded) per month and per weekday hour, and labelled hours as peak (5 a.m.-9 p.m.) or overnight.

What we see so far: the shares are stable month to month (no growing shift onto the free roads), but at the West Side Highway the excluded share almost doubles in peak hours (11.1% vs 5.9% overnight), which is the kind of time-of-day signal that toll avoidance would produce. We will treat this as a hypothesis, not proof, because the hourly mix of trip purposes also changes.

Q4. Has traffic inside the zone become faster than in 2019-2024, and than the rest of the city?

Change from proposal: The MTA speed dataset is monthly taxi/FHV speeds for three areas (CBD, CBD Adjacent, Greater NYC), not hourly speeds for all vehicles, and it currently ends in August 2025. Because 2020-2022 speeds are inflated by the pandemic, we compare against the same calendar month in 2023-2024 rather than 2019-2024; the full 2019-2025 series is still shown for context.

Transformation: for each area and calendar month we averaged 2023 and 2024 speeds as a baseline and computed the difference (mph and %) for every month.

Table. Taxi/FHV speeds, Jan-Mar 2025, vs the 2023-24 same-month baseline. Sample of 9 of 213 rows in data/processed/q4_speeds_monthly.csv.

month zone zonal_speed baseline_2023_24_mph diff_vs_baseline_mph pct_vs_baseline

2025-02-01 CBD 9.30 9.14 0.16 1.80
2025-03-01 CBD 9.28 8.91 0.37 4.20
2025-01-01 CBD Adjacent 12.93 12.86 0.07 0.50
2025-02-01 CBD Adjacent 12.67 12.84 -0.17 -1.30
2025-03-01 CBD Adjacent 12.81 12.60 0.22 1.70

2025-02-01 Greater NYC 16.76 17.02 -0.25 -1.50

What we see so far: CBD speeds were +3.1% higher in Jan-Aug 2025 than Jan-Aug 2024, while the adjacent area and the rest of the city were about 1% slower; the CBD is the only area consistently above its baseline after January 2025.

Q5 + Q7. Did crashes and injuries fall inside the zone, and did they rise just outside it?

Change from proposal: Q5 and Q7 use the same crash data with the same three-area split, so we merged them into one view. Q5's traffic part is answered by Q3/Q4 (excluded roadways and the CBD Adjacent speed series).

Transformation: downloaded all NYPD crash records since Jan 2023 (342k); dropped 20k with missing or out-of-city coordinates; assigned each crash to CRZ (inside the MTA geofence polygon), Adjacent (outside but within 1.5 km of the zone boundary: Upper East/West Side to roughly 85th St, Long Island City, Downtown Brooklyn) or Rest of NYC by point-in-polygon; aggregated to month x area (crashes, injured, killed, pedestrians, cyclists); compared the same months (Jan-Sep) each year.

What we see so far: in 2025 crashes fell 3.6% inside the zone and rose 9.2% in the adjacent ring (vs -1.5% citywide). In 2026 the CRZ is back near its 2024 level while the adjacent ring stays about 9% higher. The monthly index is noisy (e.g. a snowy February 2025), so the final view will show monthly values, not only totals.

Q6. Did more people take the subway or Citi Bike into the zone, and from which neighbourhoods?

Change from proposal: Station tap counts cannot tell where a rider is going, so we added the MTA Subway Origin-Destination Ridership Estimate (2024 and 2025) to answer the “from which neighbourhoods” part. Citi Bike monthly files are 0.4-1 GB each, so for this milestone we processed one matched pair of months (February 2024 vs February 2025).

Transformation: (1) subway hourly ridership summed to station x month and classified by station location (CRZ / Adjacent / Rest); (2) OD estimates filtered server-side with within_polygon() to weekday trips that end inside the zone and start outside it, for October 2024 and October 2025; averaged to an average weekday; origin stations joined to 2020 Neighbourhood Tabulation Areas; (3) Citi Bike: removed trips without coordinates, shorter than 1 minute or longer than 3 hours (~0.3%), kept trips ending in the zone, and grouped by start neighbourhood.

What we see so far: average weekday subway trips into the zone rose ~3.4% (985k to 1.02M) between October 2024 and October 2025, with the largest absolute gains from Brooklyn. However, station entries rose 7-9% in every area in 2025, so much of this is citywide ridership recovery. Citi Bike trips into the zone were lower in February 2025 than February 2024; one winter month is not enough, so we will add more months.

Q8. Putting it together: which areas gained, and which carried the costs?

Transformation: joined the per-area results from Q4, Q5/Q7 and Q6 into one long table (area x measure, 2024 vs 2025 over the months each dataset covers) and computed % change; for display, the sign is flipped for crashes and injuries so that green always means "better for that area".
